section: Direct Combination of Fatty Acids with Alkali.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, for the authors' improved soda-ash method of neutralising fatty acids, what are the starting solution density, the initial fraction of soda ash, and the way the remaining ash is introduced?
reference_answer: They begin with a solution of 64 deg. Tw. (35 deg. B.) made from half the requisite soda ash (9-1/2 per cent.). The remaining ash is added dry, sprinkled over each further addition of fatty acid.
required_key_points: 64 deg. Tw. (35 deg. B.)
Half the requisite soda ash (9-1/2 per cent.)
The remaining soda ash is sprinkled dry over each further addition of fatty acid
supporting_passage:
A better method of procedure, however, is to commence with a solution of
64 deg. Tw. (35 deg. B.) density, made from half the requisite soda ash (9-1/2
per cent.), and when this amount of alkali has all been taken up by the
fatty acids (which have been added gradually and with continuous
boiling), the remaining quantity of soda ash is added in a dry state,
being sprinkled over each further addition of fatty acid.

section: Saponification under Increased or Diminished Pressure.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what contrasting apparatus arrangements do the authors attribute to Haywood's and Jourdan's patents for accelerating saponification?
reference_answer: Haywood's process uses a steam-jacketed vacuum chamber with elaborate stirrers. Jourdan's lets the fat fall in a thin stream into the requisite lye already in a vessel fitted with stirring gear.
required_key_points: Haywood: a steam-jacketed vacuum chamber with an elaborate arrangement of stirrers
Jourdan: fat falls in a thin stream into the requisite lye previously placed in a vessel with stirring gear
supporting_passage:
Amongst the many attempts which have at various times
been made to shorten the process of soap-making may be mentioned
Haywood's Patent No. 759, 1901, and Jourdan's French Patent No. 339,154,
1903.

In the former, saponification is carried out in a steam-jacketed vacuum
chamber provided with an elaborate arrangement of stirrers; in the other
process fat is allowed to fall in a thin stream into the amount of lye
required for saponification, previously placed in the saponification
vessel, which is provided with stirring gear.

section: Treatment of Fat with Indefinite Amount of Alkali and no Separation of Waste Lye.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what two different rosin proportions are associated with the Soft Soap Manufacturers' Convention of Holland and the cited English patent?
reference_answer: The Dutch convention allows no more than 5 per cent. rosin, whereas the cited English patent concerns soft soap made from material containing 50 per cent. rosin.
required_key_points: Dutch convention: not more than 5 per cent. rosin
English patent: material containing 50 per cent. rosin
supporting_passage:
The Soft Soap Manufacturers' Convention of Holland stipulate that the
materials used in soft-soap making must not contain more than 5 per
cent. rosin; it is also interesting to note that a patent has been
granted (Eng. Pat. 17,278, 1900) for the manufacture of soft soap from
material containing 50 per cent. rosin.

section: Treatment of Fat with Indefinite Amount of Alkali and no Separation of Waste Lye.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, after completing saponification for smooth hydrated soap, in what sequence are the three added solutions introduced?
reference_answer: The solution of salt is added first, followed by carbonate of soda solution and finally silicate of soda solution.
required_key_points: Salt solution, then carbonate of soda solution, then silicate of soda solution
supporting_passage:
Saponification being complete, the solution of salt is
added, then the carbonate of soda solution, and finally the silicate of
soda solution, after which the soap is boiled.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, in the open-steam pasting operation, what initial caustic soda lye density and what limit on alkali addition do the authors prescribe?
reference_answer: They prescribe 14 deg. to 23.5 deg. Tw. (10 deg. to 15 deg. B.) caustic soda lye and caution against adding enough excess alkali to retard the union.
required_key_points: 14 deg. to 23.5 deg. Tw. (10 deg. to 15 deg. B.)
Alkali must not be added in sufficient excess to retard the union
supporting_passage:
The melted fats and oils are
introduced into the soap-pan and boiled by means of open steam with a
caustic soda lye 14 deg. to 23.5 deg. Tw. (10 deg. to 15 deg. B.). Whether the fatty
matters and alkali are run into the pan simultaneously or separately is
immaterial, provided the alkali is not added in sufficient excess to
retard the union.

section: Boiling on Strength or Clear Boiling.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, during boiling on strength, what concentration of caustic soda lye is specified, and how do the authors recognise the final point of lye addition?
reference_answer: They use 32-1/2 deg. Tw., 20 deg. B. lye. Addition ends when the caustic soda or "strength" remains permanent, the mass no longer absorbs more, and it is thrown out of solution and grained.
required_key_points: 32-1/2 deg. Tw., 20 deg. B.
The caustic soda or "strength" remains permanent and the mass refuses to absorb more
The soapy mass is thrown out of solution and grained
supporting_passage:
Caustic soda lye (32-1/2 deg. Tw., 20 deg. B.) is gradually added until the soap
is again opened or grained, and boiling continued by the use of the dry
steam coil. As soon as the caustic soda lye is absorbed, another portion
is slowly added, and this is continued until the caustic soda or
"strength" remains permanent and the soapy mass, refusing to absorb
more, is thrown out of solution and grained.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, when checking the fit of boiled soap with a sideways-held hot trowel, what two features of the soap film indicate the proper condition?
reference_answer: The soap film should fall from the trowel in two or three flakes and leave the trowel surface clean and dry.
required_key_points: The thin layer drops off in two or three flakes
The trowel surface is left clean and dry
supporting_passage:
Samples are tested from time to time as to their behaviour in dropping
off a hot trowel held sideways; the thin layer should drop off in two or
three flakes and leave the surface of the trowel clean and dry.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what different outcomes do the authors associate with boiling curd-mottled soap too long as opposed to too briefly?
reference_answer: Boiling too long prevents the mottling from forming properly; insufficient boiling leaves an excess of entangled lye in the soap.
required_key_points: Too long: the mottling will not form properly
Insufficient boiling: the soap contains an excess of entangled lye
supporting_passage:
If boiled too long the mottling will not form
properly, and, on the other hand, insufficient boiling will cause the
soap to contain an excess of entangled lye.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, for one ton of blue-mottled soap and one ton of grey-mottled soap, which colouring agent and amount do the authors give for each?
reference_answer: They specify 3-4 lb. ultramarine for blue mottled soap, and 1-3 lb. manganese dioxide for grey mottled soap.
required_key_points: Blue: 3-4 lb. ultramarine
Grey: 1-3 lb. manganese dioxide
supporting_passage:
When this mottling condition has been obtained, the colouring matter,
which would be ultramarine for the blue mottled and manganese dioxide
for the grey mottled soap (3-4 lb. ultramarine or 1-3 lb. manganese
dioxide being sufficient for 1 ton of soap), is mixed with a little
water and added to the boiling soap--the boiling is continued until all
is thoroughly amalgamated, and when the steam is shut off the contents
of the pan are ready for cleansing.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, in making a milling base from tallow and cocoa-nut oil, what sequence do the authors require before starting boiling on strength?
reference_answer: They thoroughly saponify the tallow first and grain it with caustic soda lye rather than salt. They then withdraw the half-spent lyes, add the cocoa-nut oil, and saponify it.
required_key_points: Saponify the tallow first and grain with caustic soda lye rather than salt
Withdraw the half-spent lyes
Add and saponify the cocoa-nut oil
supporting_passage:
The tallow is thoroughly saponified first,
and the graining is performed by the aid of caustic soda lye in
preference to salt. The half-spent lyes are withdrawn, and the cocoa-nut
oil added to the pan. This is saponified, and when the saponification is
complete, "boiling-on-strength" is proceeded with.

section: Resting of Pans and Settling of Soap.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, after a fitted pan settles, what average fatty-acid content and what approximate share of the total soap do the authors assign to the nigre layer?
reference_answer: The nigre layer averages 33 per cent. fatty acids and accounts for 15-20 per cent. of the total soap in the pan.
required_key_points: 33 per cent. fatty acids
15-20 per cent. of the total soap in the pan
supporting_passage:
A layer of darker weak soap, termed "nigre," which on an average
tests 33 per cent. fatty acids, and, according to the particular fit
employed, will amount to from 15-20 per cent. of the total quantity of
soap in the pan.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, in the described method for bleaching nigre with stannous chloride, what solution strength and treatment proportions are specified?
reference_answer: The specified strength is a 20 per cent. solution, with 1 cwt. of the solution sufficient to bleach 20 tons of nigre.
required_key_points: 20 per cent. solution
1 cwt. of solution for 20 tons of nigre
supporting_passage:
Nigre may be bleached by treatment with a 20 per cent. solution of
stannous chloride--1 cwt. of this solution (previously heated) is
sufficient to bleach 20 tons of nigre.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what substance do the authors say Zelinsky obtained on heating a petroleum-derived acid with glycerine, and what were its properties?
reference_answer: The product was tri-octin, which had the properties of a fat.
required_key_points: Tri-octin
It had the properties of a fat
supporting_passage:
In this connection may be quoted the interesting work of Zelinsky
(_Russ. Phys. Chem. Ges. Zeits. Angew. Chem._, 1903, 37). He obtained
substances, by acting with carbon dioxide upon magnesia compounds of
chlorinated fractions of petroleum, which when decomposed by dilute
sulphuric acid, yielded various organic acids. One of these acids on
heating with glycerine formed tri-octin, which had the properties of a
fat.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how did Merry and Noble's electrical soap-making patent generate and apply the alkali to the fat?
reference_answer: Merry and Noble produced caustic alkali electrolytically from brine and deposited it on wire-netting in the presence of fat.
required_key_points: Caustic alkali was produced electrolytically from brine
The alkali was deposited on wire-netting in the presence of fat
supporting_passage:
Attempts have been made to produce
soap electrically by Messrs. Nodon, Brettonneau and Shee (Eng. Pat.
22,129, 1897), and also by Messrs. Merry and Noble (Eng. Pat. 2,372,
1900).

In the former patent, a mixture of soda-lye and fat is agitated by
electricity at a temperature of 194 deg.-212 deg. F. (90 deg.-100
deg. C.), while in the latter caustic alkali is electrolytically
produced from brine, and deposited on wire-netting in the presence
of fat, which is thereby saponified.

section: Treatment of Fat with Definite Amount of Alkali and no Separation of Waste Lye.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what processing temperatures do the authors allow for cold-process soap made only with cocoa-nut oil versus mixtures containing tallow?
reference_answer: For cocoa-nut oil alone they give 75 deg. F. (24 deg. C.); for mixtures containing tallow they give 100 deg. to 120 deg. F. (38 deg. to 49 deg. C.).
required_key_points: Cocoa-nut oil alone: 75 deg. F. (24 deg. C.)
Mixtures containing tallow: 100 deg. to 120 deg. F. (38 deg. to 49 deg. C.)
supporting_passage:
The temperature, which, of course, must vary with the season, should be
as low as is consistent with fluidity, and for cocoa-nut oil alone may
be 75 deg. F. (24 deg. C.), but in mixtures containing tallow 100 deg. to 120 deg. F.
(38 deg. to 49 deg. C.).

section: Treatment of Fat with Indefinite Amount of Alkali and no Separation of Waste Lye.
question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, when caustic soda lye is added to potash lye for soft soap during hot weather, what proportion is described, and what effects are warned of if there is even a slight excess?
reference_answer: The caustic soda lye is used to the extent of one-fourth; even a slight excess produces a bad appearance and a tendency for the soap to separate.
required_key_points: To the extent of one-fourth
A bad appearance
A tendency to separate
supporting_passage:
Caustic soda lye is sometimes admixed, to the extent of one-fourth, with
potash lye to keep the soap firmer during hot weather, but it requires
great care, as a slight excess of soda gives soft soap a bad appearance
and a tendency to separate.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what observation in a sample taken on a wooden trowel shows that enough salt or brine has been added during graining out?
reference_answer: The sample has distinct grains of soap alongside a liquid portion that separates easily.
required_key_points: Distinct grains of soap
A liquid portion that will easily separate
supporting_passage:
When a sample, taken out on a wooden trowel, consists of distinct grains
of soap and a liquid portion, which will easily separate, sufficient
salt or brine has been added; the boiling is stopped and the spent lye
allowed to settle out, whilst the soap remains on the surface as a more
or less thick mass.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, how long do the authors leave a finished batch of curd soap covered in the pan before transferring it to frames?
reference_answer: They leave the covered pan to rest for eight to ten hours.
required_key_points: Eight to ten hours
supporting_passage:
Boiling is then stopped, and, after covering, the pan is allowed
to rest for eight to ten hours, when the soap is ready for filling into
frames, where it is crutched until perfectly smooth.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, what regional names do the authors report for the finest yellow household bar soap in the South and West versus the North of England?
reference_answer: In the South and West it is called Primrose Soap; in the North the authors give names such as Golden Pale.
required_key_points: South and West: Primrose Soap
North: any of Golden Pale, Imperial Pale, or Gold Medal Pale
supporting_passage:
The best quality is
known in the South and West of England as Primrose Soap, but is
designated in the North of England by such names as Golden Pale,
Imperial Pale, Gold Medal Pale, etc.

question: In The Handbook of Soap Manufacture by W. H. Simmons and H. A. Appleton, when making the cane-sugar solution for the transparent-soap recipe, what weights of sugar and water are used and at what temperature are they dissolved?
reference_answer: The recipe uses 50 lb. cane sugar dissolved in 50 lb. water at 168 deg. F. (76 deg. C.).
required_key_points: 50 lb. cane sugar
50 lb. water
168 deg. F. (76 deg. C.)
supporting_passage:
Whilst saponification is proceeding, the "sugar solution" is prepared by
dissolving 50 lb. cane sugar in 50 lb. water, at 168 deg. F. (76 deg. C.), to
which may be added 5 lb. soda crystals, and any necessary colouring
matter.
